en: Thus have I heard: the Discourse on All Taints (Sabbāsavasutta), the second in the Middle Length Discourses (Majjhima Nikāya).
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the method for the restraint of all taints.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints occurs for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.
And what, monks, is it that one must know and see for the destruction of the taints to occur?
It is wise attention and unwise attention.”
“Monks, for one who attends to things improperly, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase.
But for one who attends to things properly, monks, unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.
There are, monks, taints to be abandoned by vision; there are taints to be abandoned by restraint; there are taints...”
There are taints to be abandoned by avoidance; there are taints to be abandoned by endurance; there are taints to be abandoned by shunning;
there are taints to be abandoned by removal; there are taints to be abandoned by cultivation.
1. Taints to be abandoned by vision.
And what, monks, are the taints that are to be abandoned by vision?

Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—does not understand the things that should be attended to, and does not understand the things that should not be attended to.

Thus, not understanding the things that should be attended to and not understanding the things that should not be attended to, one attends to those things that should not be attended to, and does not attend to those things that should be attended to.
And what, monks, are the things that should not be attended to which one attends to?
Those things, monks, by attending to which the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, or the arisen taint of sensual desire increases.
The taint of existence that has not yet arisen arises, or the taint of existence that has already arisen increases;
the taint of ignorance that has not yet arisen arises, or the taint of ignorance that has already arisen increases—
these are the phenomena that he attends to, which are not [normally] to be attended to.
And what, monks, are those things that should be attended to, which he does not attend to?
Monks, when one attends to these things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise, and the arisen taint of sensual desire is abandoned;
the unarisen taint of existence does not arise, and the arisen taint of existence is abandoned.
“Unarisen taints of ignorance do not arise, or arisen taints of ignorance are abandoned”—
these are the things that should be attended to, yet he does not attend to them.
Because he attends to things that should not be attended to and does not attend to things that should be attended to, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase.
Thus he attends to it in an improper manner:
"Did I exist in the past? Or did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past?"
Was I in the past?
Shall I indeed exist in the future? Or shall I not exist in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? What...
Having sacrificed, one wonders: "What indeed will I become in the future time?
Or, regarding the present internal time, one is full of doubt:
"Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come? Where will it go?"
As he attends to this in an improper way, one of six views arises in him.
Either the view “I have a self” arises in him as a truth and a certainty,
or the view “I have no self” arises in him as a truth and a certainty.
Or else, the view arises in him as something true and certain: "I perceive self by means of self";
or the view arises in him as something true and certain: "I perceive not-self by means of self";
or the view arises in him as something true and certain: "I perceive self by means of not-self."
Or else he holds such a view as this:
"This self of mine—which speaks and experiences, which undergoes here and there the results of good and evil deeds—is indeed my self;
it is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain exactly so for all eternity."
This, monks, is called a way of views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views.
Bound by the fetter of views, monks, the uninstructed worldling is not freed from birth, aging, and death; not freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
I say he is not freed from suffering.
But the learned noble disciple, monks— seeing the noble ones,
skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; seeing true persons, skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, well-trained in the Dhamma of true persons—
understands the states that should be attended to and understands the states that should not be attended to.

Thus, understanding the phenomena that should be attended to and understanding the phenomena that should not be attended to, he does not attend to those phenomena that should not be attended to, and he attends to those phenomena that should be attended to.
And what, monks, are the phenomena that should not be attended to, which he does not attend to?
Those phenomena, monks, by attending to which the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, or the arisen taint of sensual desire increases.
Either the taint of existence that has not yet arisen arises, or the taint of existence that has already arisen increases;
either the taint of ignorance that has not yet arisen arises, or the taint of ignorance that has already arisen increases—
these are the phenomena that are not to be attended to, which he does not attend to.
"And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be attended to, which he attends to?
When he attends to those things, bhikkhus, the unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise, and the arisen taint of sensual desire is abandoned;
the unarisen taint of existence does not arise, and the arisen taint of existence is abandoned."
Either the unarisen taint of ignorance does not arise, or the arisen taint of ignorance is abandoned—
these are the phenomena that should be attended to, which he attends to.
By not attending to those phenomena that should not be attended to, and by attending to those phenomena that should be attended to, both unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
Thus he attends wisely: “This is suffering”; he attends wisely: “This is the origin of suffering”; he attends wisely:
“This is the cessation of suffering”; he attends wisely: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
As he attends wisely in this way, three fetters are abandoned:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by seeing.
2. Taints to be Abandoned by Restraint.
And what, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells reflecting wisely, restrained with restraint over the faculty of the eye.

“Monks, those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise in one who dwells without restraint over the faculty of the eye do not occur for one who dwells with restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Reflecting wisely, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the faculty of the ear … [and so on] … he dwells restrained by the restraint of the faculty of the nose … [and so on] …”
He dwells restrained by the restraint of the tongue-faculty …pe… he dwells restrained by the restraint of the body-faculty …pe… he dwells restrained by the restraint of the mind-faculty.

“Monks, whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise in one who dwells unrestrained in the faculty of the mind—those taints, vexations, and fevers do not arise for one who dwells restrained in the faculty of the mind.
Whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise in one who dwells unrestrained in restraint—those taints, vexations, and fevers do not arise for one who dwells restrained in restraint.
These, monks, are called the taints that are to be abandoned by restraint.”
3. Taints to be Abandoned by Use.
And what, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by use?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, uses his robe: [text continues]

‘Only for the removal of hunger and for the warding off of cold, for the warding off of heat, for the warding off of contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and only for the purpose of covering the private parts.
Reflecting wisely, he uses almsfood:
‘Neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for smartening, nor for adornment, but only for the maintenance of this body.’

"For the sake of maintaining this life, for the cessation of harm, and for the support of the holy life—thus I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings; and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a state of ease.
Thus, he uses his lodging with wise reflection.

‘Only for the warding off of cold, for the warding off of heat, for the warding off of contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things; only for the purpose of removing the distress of the seasons and for delighting in seclusion.
He uses the requisite of medicine and provisions for the sick after wise reflection:
‘Only for the warding off of arisen afflictive feelings, for the sake of supreme health.’
“Monks, those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise from not using [certain things] do not exist for one who uses them.
These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by use.
4. Taints to be Abandoned by Forbearance”
"And what, bhikkhus, are the taints that are to be abandoned by endurance?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, is patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things; he is patient with abusive and unwelcome modes of speech."
He is one who is accustomed to enduring arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
For those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise in one who does not endure them do not exist for him when he endures them.
These, monks, are called the taints that are to be abandoned by endurance. And what,
monks, are the taints that are to be abandoned by avoidance?
In this case, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, avoids a fierce elephant,
avoids a fierce horse, avoids a fierce bull, avoids a fierce dog; he avoids snakes,
stumps, thorny places, pits, precipices, cesspools, and drains.
If there were a certain kind of improper seat, a certain kind of improper resort,
or a certain kind of evil companions that wise fellow-celibates might regard as grounds for censure,
he reflects wisely and avoids that improper seat, that improper resort, and those evil companions.
“Monks, those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise for one who does not avoid them do not exist for one who avoids them.
These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by avoidance.
6. Taints to be abandoned by removal.”
"And what, monks, are the taints that are to be abandoned by removal?
Here, monks, a monk, reflecting thoroughly, does not tolerate a thought of sensual desire that has arisen;
he abandons it, removes it, makes an end of it, and brings it to non-existence. [He does not tolerate] a thought of ill will that has arisen... a thought of cruelty that has arisen."
...pe... whatever evil, unwholesome states arise, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
For those taints, afflictions, and fevers that would arise for one who does not dispel them—those very taints, afflictions, and fevers do not exist for one who dispels them.
These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by dispelling.
7. Taints to be Abandoned by Cultivation.
And what, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by cultivation?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, develops the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
Reflecting wisely, he develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena … he develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture …
He develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility… he develops the enlightenment factor of concentration… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity,
which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
"Monks, those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise for one who does not cultivate [the path] do not exist for one who cultivates it.
These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by cultivation.
Now, monks, when a monk has abandoned through vision those taints that are to be abandoned by vision..."
Those taints that are to be abandoned by restraint have been abandoned by restraint; those taints that are to be abandoned by avoidance have been abandoned by avoidance;
those taints that are to be abandoned by endurance have been abandoned by endurance;
those taints that are to be abandoned by evasion have been abandoned by evasion; those taints that are to be abandoned by removal...
“Those taints that are to be abandoned by avoidance have been abandoned by avoidance; those taints that are to be abandoned by cultivation have been abandoned by cultivation.

This, monks, is called a monk who dwells restrained by the restraint of all taints: he has cut off craving, he has removed the fetters, and through the complete penetration of conceit, he has made an end of suffering.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The second discourse, “All Taints,” is concluded.
